title: Islands in a grid
objectives: Treat a grid as a graph to count islands.
Mark visited cells without changing the caller's grid

screens.title: Walking on land
screens.prose: Each cell is land (1) or water (0). You can step between two land cells only if they share a side. An **island** is all the land you can reach that way.
screens.question: Tap every cell of the island that holds the marked cell.

hints.text: From the marked cell, step up, down, left or right onto land.
The marked cell has land above it and to its left.
r1c5 is above, r2c4 is to the left. r3c3 touches r2c4 only at a corner, so it is not reachable.

feedback.correct: Three cells: the marked one, the one above and the one to its left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step only through shared sides, and tap every land cell you reach.

byKey.diag: You added r3c3. It touches r2c4 only at a corner, and a step needs a shared side.
byKey.r3c3: r3c3 touches the island only at a corner, so you cannot step onto it.
byKey.r1c5: r1c5 is directly above the marked cell, so it belongs to the island.

explain.text: Treat each land cell as a node with up to four neighbours: up, down, left and right. The island is the connected component of the marked cell. A search from it finds exactly these three cells.

screens.title: How many islands
screens.prose: The same map. Land counts as one island only when side-to-side steps join it.
screens.question: How many islands does the map hold?

hints.text: Go cell by cell. Each time you meet land you have not counted, count one island and colour all of it.
The single cells r3c3 and r5c4 touch other land only at corners.
Top left 3 cells, top right 3, r3c3, bottom left 3, bottom right 3, and r5c4: 6 islands.

feedback.correct: Six islands, two of them a single cell.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Join land only through shared sides, then count the groups.

byKey.diag: You joined cells that meet at a corner. r3c3 and r5c4 are islands on their own.
byKey.cells: You counted land cells. Count groups of joined cells instead.

explain.text: You scanned the grid and started a new island at each unseen land cell. That is the component counter from lesson 3, with grid cells as nodes. Each search must mark what it reaches, or the next land cell is counted again.

screens.title: A cell's neighbours
screens.prose: In code the grid is a list of rows, and a cell is `(r, c)` counted from 0. A cell on the edge has fewer than four neighbours.
screens.question: Write `neighbours(r, c, rows, cols)`: the cells sharing a side with `(r, c)` inside the grid, in the order up, down, left, right.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: a middle cell, corners, a single row and a 1 by 1 grid. Return (row, col) tuples in the order up, down, left, right.

hints.text: Try all four steps, then keep only those inside the grid.
The top-left cell `(0, 0)` has just two neighbours.
For `(dr, dc)` in `((-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1))`: keep `(r + dr, c + dc)` when `0 <= r + dr < rows` and `0 <= c + dc < cols`.

feedback.correct: Four steps, each checked against the edges.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is the corner `(0, 0)`. Up and left fall off the grid; a negative index would wrap round in Python.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 is a middle cell, with all four. Keep the order up, down, left, right, and no diagonals.

explain.text: Python reads `grid[-1]` as the last row, so a missing bounds check wraps round silently instead of failing. Checking both bounds keeps every step on the map.

screens.title: What it costs
screens.prose: The outer loop scans every cell once. Each land cell is pushed once, and when popped it looks at up to 4 neighbours.
screens.question: On a 1,000 by 1,000 grid of all land, how many neighbour looks happen at most?

hints.text: How many cells are there, and how many looks does each make?
Each cell is popped once.
$1{,}000 \times 1{,}000 = 10^6$ cells, times 4 looks each, is $4 \times 10^6$.

feedback.correct: $4 \times 10^6$: linear in the number of cells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the number of cells by the looks per cell.

byKey.cells: That counts the cells. Each popped cell then looks at up to 4 neighbours.
byKey.pairs: That pairs every cell with every other, as a matrix would. A cell only looks at its 4 neighbours.

explain.text: The work is $O(rc)$ for an $r \times c$ grid: each cell is scanned once and searched from once. We never build an adjacency list; the neighbours come from arithmetic on `(r, c)`.

screens.title: Count the islands
screens.prose: The convention here: **do not change `grid`**, because the caller still needs it. Keep a `seen` set of cells instead of overwriting land.
screens.question: Write `count_islands(grid)`: the number of islands of 1s, joined through shared sides.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests: the map above, an empty grid, one cell, all water and diagonal cells. Others have a single row, one big island and a ring, and one checks that `grid` is unchanged afterwards.

hints.text: Scan every cell. At unseen land, count one and search the whole island.
An empty grid has no first row, so `len(grid[0])` would fail.
`rows = len(grid)`, `cols = len(grid[0]) if rows else 0`. At each unseen 1, add 1 and run a stack search marking `(r, c)` in `seen`.

feedback.correct: One search per island, each cell seen once, and the input untouched.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: Test 5 is two cells meeting at a corner: two islands. Use only the four side neighbours.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 checks the grid afterwards. You set land to 0, so the caller's map was wiped. Use a `seen` set.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 is a 20 by 20 island of 400 cells. The answer is 1.

explain.text: Marking a cell when it is pushed stops double counting and repeat work. The `seen` set costs $O(rc)$ memory but leaves the map as the caller passed it. The stack avoids recursion depth limits on big islands.

screens.title: Sinking the caller's map
screens.prose:
A common shortcut marks land by sinking it: `grid[r][c] = 0`. This version counts correctly.

```python
book = [[1, 1, 0],
        [0, 0, 1]]
n = count_islands(book)
print(n, book)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected the function to get its own copy. Python passes the same list, so `grid[r][c] = 0` sinks the caller's land.
Each island is counted before it is sunk, so the count is still 2. Only the map is damaged.

hints.text: Is `grid` inside the function a copy of `book`, or the same list?
These land cells are set to 0 by the search.
The function gets the same list object, so every land cell of `book` is now 0. The count is right: 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the function sees a copy or the caller's own list.

byKey.kept: You assumed the function works on a copy. It changes `book` itself, so the land is gone afterwards.

explain.text: Sinking saves the `seen` set's memory but destroys the input. If you want it, copy first with `g = [row[:] for row in grid]`. `grid.copy()` is not enough: it copies the outer list, and the rows are still shared.

screens.title: One long island
screens.prose: A recursive flood fill calls itself on each land neighbour. On a 300 by 300 grid of all land, the search snakes through every cell, each call inside the last.

state.caption: On a 4 by 4 grid the dive passes all 16 cells

screens.question: How many calls are open at the deepest point?

options.text: About 90,000, far past Python's limit of about 1,000

options.why: Each call waits for its neighbours' calls to finish. So the frames stack up along the whole path.
The dive goes down one column, up the next and so on, through all 90,000 cells in one chain.

hints.text: Follow the path drawn on the small grid. Does any call return before the end?
On 4 by 4, all 16 calls are open at the end.
On 300 by 300 the dive passes all $300^2 = 90{,}000$ cells before any call returns.

feedback.correct: Recursion depth equals the length of the dive: here every cell.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls still waiting when the dive reaches its last cell.

explain.text: One big island makes the recursion as deep as the island is large. That is why the solution above uses an explicit stack. A queue works just as well: BFS on a grid is also $O(rc)$.

screens.title: The grid pattern
screens.question: Which cells are neighbours of $(r, c)$ in this pattern?

options.text: $(r-1, c)$, $(r+1, c)$, $(r, c-1)$, $(r, c+1)$, when inside the grid
All 8 surrounding cells, when inside the grid
options.why: That joins cells meeting at a corner, which merged r3c3 into its neighbour earlier. Islands here use shared sides only.

options.text: The 4 side cells, wrapping round the edges
options.why: Wrapping would join the left edge to the right edge. Python's negative indexes do this by accident without a bounds check.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two cells join only through a shared side.

explain.text: Some problems do count corners; then the step list has 8 entries and nothing else changes. The scan, the `seen` set and the search stay the same.

screens.title: Loss regions on a P&L surface
screens.prose: Risk grids an options book's P&L over spot and volatility moves. A **loss region** is a side-joined group of scenarios losing more than the limit. Each region is a separate group of losing scenarios.

state.caption: P&L of a short straddle book, £k, for each scenario

screens.question: Write `count_loss_regions(pnl, limit)`: the number of regions where P&L is below −limit.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. A cell is a loss cell when its P&L is strictly below −limit, in £k. Cells join only through a shared side.

hints.text: Turn the test into a land check: a cell is land when `pnl[r][c] < -limit`.
With a £50k limit only these four corner cells lose too much.
Copy your island counter and replace `grid[r][c] == 1` with `pnl[r][c] < -limit` in both places.

feedback.correct: The island counter, with a threshold as the land test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 uses a £50k limit: a crash with vol up, and a rally with vol up. That is 2 regions.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 uses £10k. The vol-up column links the two corners, so there is 1 region.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 checks the boundary: −50 is not below −50, so only −51 counts.

explain.text: At £50k the book loses in two separate places: a sharp fall or a sharp rise, each with vol up. At £10k the +4 vol column loses everywhere, joining them into one region. So the count depends on the limit as well as on the book.

ideas: A grid is a graph: each cell is a node, joined to the cells sharing a side. Find them by arithmetic on `(r, c)` with a bounds check.
Counting islands is counting components: scan every cell, and start a search at each unseen land cell. It costs $O(rc)$.
Mark cells in a `seen` set when pushed, so nothing is counted twice and the caller's grid is left alone. Use a stack, not recursion, for big islands.

formula.name: Island count cost
formula.note: Each cell is scanned once and searched from once.

summary.trap: Counting diagonal cells as neighbours merges islands that only touch at a corner.

quiz.prose: You threshold a 50-stock correlation matrix: cell $(i, j)$ is 1 when stocks $i$ and $j$ have correlation above 0.8. You want clusters of correlated stocks.
quiz.question: Which method is right?

options.text: Treat it as an adjacency matrix: stock $i$ links to each $j$ with a 1 in row $i$; count components
Count islands of 1s with 4 side neighbours
options.why: Cells $(i, j)$ and $(i, j+1)$ are two unrelated pairs of stocks. The matrix's layout is not a map.

options.text: Count the rows that contain a 1
options.why: That counts stocks with at least one partner, not the clusters they form.

feedback.correct: The thresholded matrix is a graph's adjacency matrix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a cell of this matrix stands for.

explain.text: A cell here is a pair of stocks, not a place. Neighbouring cells mean nothing. Run lesson 3's component counter over the stocks.

quiz.question: How many islands, joining cells through shared sides only?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether any two land cells share a side.

byKey.diag: You joined the cells through their corners. No two land cells here share a side.

explain.text: Every 1 touches the others only at corners. So each is its own island: 5 in all.

quiz.prose: Three ways to mark cells during the island search.
quiz.question: Which avoids double counting and leaves the caller's grid unchanged?

options.text: Add `(r, c)` to a `seen` set when it is pushed

options.why: That avoids double counting but sinks the caller's map.

options.text: Mark nothing; the outer loop skips water anyway
options.why: Then the search steps back and forth between two land cells forever, and the outer loop counts each island again.

feedback.correct: A separate `seen` set does both jobs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need a mark that lives outside the grid.

explain.text: A `seen` set records visits without touching `grid`. It costs up to $O(rc)$ memory, the price of keeping the input intact.

quiz.prose: A grid with a single row: `[[1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]]`.
quiz.question: How many islands?

feedback.correct: Runs of 1s: 2 cells, 1 cell and 3 cells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count runs of 1s separated by 0s.

byKey.cells: You counted land cells. Joined cells form one island.

explain.text: In one row, the only neighbours are left and right. So each run of 1s is an island: 3 runs.
